1.0.0.en: The Medes: the inhabitants of the kingdom of Media, which is bounded on the north and east by the Caspian Sea, on the south by Persia, and on the west by the kingdom of Assyria (present-day Iraq). Arphaxad is the one called "Phraortes," that is, "the great king," or "Phra," that is, king, to which "Kshad," that is, "the gentle," was then added. All of these are names of one king, who was titled the great and gentle king. He was great because he built the great city "Achmetha," and gentle because he loved the Jews and was kind to them. He was the son of King "Deioces," who began the building of Achmetha, and then Arphaxad completed its building.

1.0.1.en: It is evident that this Arphaxad was strong and great, and was able to triumph over many peoples around him and to enlarge the kingdom of "Media."

1.0.2.en: To confirm his greatness he built a great city which he called "Achmetha," or "Ecbatana," and made it the capital of the land of Media. It is near the present city of Tehran in Iran.

1.1.0.en: The great King Arphaxad took care to build his capital Achmetha with the highest degree of strength and grandeur. He built its houses of squared blocks of stone and made its walls very high and massive, proclaiming the impregnability of his city and his power. The height of the wall was seventy cubits (the cubit ranges between

1.1.1.en: 45-50 cm) – that is, the cubit of a man – or about thirty-five meters, while the breadth of the wall was thirty cubits, or about fifteen meters approximately, so that the wall became like a broad road on which chariots and soldiers could be assembled.

1.1.2.en: To magnify his city he built towers on the wall, reaching a height of one hundred cubits, or about fifty meters. They were square towers, each side about twenty feet long (the foot being 30 cm), that is, about six meters.

1.1.3.en: As for the gates of the city, he made them very high and massive like towers, reaching a height of fifty meters, so that the greatness of his armies would be seen when they marched out of them. And Arphaxad became haughty and boasted of his power and the greatness of his armies.

1.1.4.en: This is man in every generation: he relies on material things and thinks by this that he has fortified himself, but "Except the Lord keep the house, the watchman waketh but in vain" (Ps 126:1-2). This great city was destroyed shortly afterward, just as all the material things on which man relies vanish, and nothing remains except "the name of the Lord, which is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe" (Prov 18:10). So I wish, my brother, that you would be humble and thank God for His gifts, and not exalt yourself over those around you, but be like your Master, who sat at the feet of His disciples.

1.2.s.en: (2) The victory of Nabuchodonosor over Arphaxad

1.2.0.en: Tigris and Euphrates: the two main rivers of Iraq.

1.2.1.en: Jadason: a river located in the east of Iraq.

1.2.2.en: Elymeans: that is, Elam, a country located east of Iraq.

1.2.3.en: Ragau: that is, Rhages. This region is located east of Iraq, at the border of the king of the Elymeans.

1.2.4.en: Nabuchodonosor, king of Assyria (which neighbors Media on the west), whose capital was Nineveh (located on the river Tigris), feared the growing power of Arphaxad and his control over the neighboring kingdoms. So in the twelfth year of his reign Nabuchodonosor decided to make war against Arphaxad, king of Media. He is not the same as Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who came at a later time and defeated the kingdom of Assyria, since Nebuchadnezzar is a title given to some of the kings of Assyria and Babylon and means "protector of the land," and his real name was "Esarhaddon." So he marched toward Arphaxad with great armies and met him in the plain of "Ragau."

1.2.5.en: The wars between Nabuchodonosor and Arphaxad continued for five years, until the seventeenth year of Nabuchodonosor's reign (according to the modern edition of the Jesuit Fathers). In the end he triumphed over him and took possession of his land.

1.3.s.en: (3) The messages of Nabuchodonosor to the lands of the West

1.3.0.en: Cilicia: a province located in the southeast of Asia Minor, that is, Turkey.

1.3.1.en: Damascus: the capital of present-day Syria, an ancient city from the days of our father Abraham.

1.3.2.en: Lebanon: the present country of Lebanon, which lies on the Mediterranean Sea, north of Jordan and Palestine.

1.3.3.en: Nabuchodonosor repeated the error of Arphaxad: he became proud and sought to dominate the lands of the world around him. So he sent messengers to the lands of Cilicia, Damascus and Lebanon, that is, what corresponds today to the region of Turkey, Syria and Lebanon.

1.4.0.en: Carmel: a mountain range located east of Lebanon.

1.4.1.en: Cedar: one of the most important Arab tribes that dwelt in the north of the Arabian Peninsula, that is, present-day Saudi Arabia.

1.4.2.en: Galilee: the northern region of the land of the Jews, that is, Canaan, and most of its inhabitants were Gentiles. Esdraelon: a region located in the north of Galilee.

1.4.3.en: He also sent to the regions of Carmel, Cedar, Galilee and Esdraelon, that is, what corresponds today to Lebanon, northern Saudi Arabia and northern Palestine.

1.5.0.en: Samaria: a fortified city to which many lands were subject, located in the middle part of the land of the Jews, that is, ancient Canaan, between Galilee in the north and Judea in the south. It was the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel when it was divided in the days of Rehoboam the son of Solomon.

1.5.1.en: Beyond Jordan to Jerusalem: this includes all the lands surrounding the river Jordan and extends to the north of Egypt. Its most important city is Jerusalem, which lies southwest of the Jordan.

1.5.2.en: The land of Jesse: the whole land of the Jews, which expanded in the days of King David the son of Jesse and extends from the river Jordan to the borders of Egypt.

1.5.3.en: He also sent to the land of Samaria and the regions surrounding the river Jordan as far as the borders of Egypt and Ethiopia, that is, he sent to all the lands of the Jews and also to Ethiopia. So the king's messengers reached all the lands mentioned above.

1.5.4.en: So it is that pride is the mother of many sins: it leads to greed, the exploitation of others, and contempt for them. Therefore humility is also the father of many virtues, and it – that is, humility – is greatly hated by Satan, because it gives man the joy of fellowship with God through various virtues.

1.6.0.en: When the messages of Nabuchodonosor reached all the lands, they too fell into pride and made light of him. They agreed not to submit to him, and drove out his messengers with contempt, relying on their own strength and despising him. This was the way known at that time to express objection to messages: insulting those who carried them.

1.7.0.en: When the messengers returned to Nabuchodonosor, he was very angry and swore by his throne that he would take vengeance on all these lands. This shows his pride, which inclines toward deifying himself: he does not swear by the pagan gods, but swears by his throne and his authority.

1.7.1.en: So they met his pride with their own pride, and of course pride does not cure pride, but rather inflames it more. The only solution is humility, so that God's mercies overflow upon the humble man and he overcomes all his enemies, just as Christ – by His humility on the cross – conquered all the pride of the devil and his authority.

1.7.2.en: The army advanced on the surrounding countries

2.0.s.en: (1) The king's decision to take possession of all the earth

2.0.0.en: The first month: that is, the month of Nisan, which corresponds to the present month of April. This month is the first in the Babylonian year.

2.0.1.en: After the reign of Nabuchodonosor king of Assyria was established and he had triumphed over Arphaxad king of the Medes, he resolved in himself to take vengeance on all the lands that had refused to submit to him. In his pride he wanted to occupy the whole world around him and set himself up as a god over the peoples. He chose a suitable time to prepare the army and attack, which was the season of spring, so this agreement took place in the month of April.

2.1.0.en: He communicated his secret counsel to them: he agreed with them on a plan of war.

2.1.1.en: The king gathered his counselors, the elders, and likewise the commanders of his armies, and agreed with them on a plan of war to take vengeance on all his enemies who had refused to submit to him and to receive his messengers.

2.2.0.en: The king agreed with his counselors and his commanders on his decision, which he had taken in himself in pride, to subject the whole world to himself.

2.2.1.en: This is the insatiable greed of man: whenever God gives him a grace, he asks for more. He does not thank God but grows more boastful of himself, and in the end he loses everything, because he did not know the source of his grace, that is, God, and did not delight in fellowship with Him.

2.3.s.en: (2) Preparing the army and its needs

2.3.0.en: Holofernes: a Persian name meaning God appeared, or revealed.

2.3.1.en: The king's counselors and the commander of his armies were pleased with the king's idea of founding an empire that would subject the whole world to itself. It seems that the king's pride and conceit passed to his helpers, so they praised his idea and supported it with all their hearts, which led him to go further and take practical steps. He summoned the greatest of his military commanders – perhaps he had not been present at this session because of special circumstances, or he was present and the king took him aside to give him specific orders regarding his desire to subject the whole world to himself – so that he would attack all the cities around him throughout the inhabited world, fortified and unfortified, and destroy them violently, especially those who had made light of his messengers and refused to submit to him. Most of these kingdoms lie to the west of Assyria.

2.3.2.en: So it is with man: when he is enraged he rushes into actions that may seem logical although they are wrong and spring from the pride of his heart, because "the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:20). Beware, then, of taking any decision when you are angry; rather wait until you calm down, then pray and make your decisions.

2.4.0.en: Holofernes the commander began to prepare the army. He gathered one hundred and twenty thousand fighting men on foot, and of the horsemen able to use arrows and bows he gathered twelve thousand, so that he had a great and mighty army. In his pride he felt able to subdue the whole earth, forgetting that there is a power greater than he, which is God.

2.5.1.en: Holofernes began to gather provisions for his long journey. He gathered camels, cattle and sheep that were hard to count, to supply his soldiers with rich food, bearing in mind that the huge number of the army needed no fewer than four thousand sheep daily to feed it, or the equivalent in cattle and other kinds of livestock. Thus we can imagine the enormity of the herds that accompanied this mighty army. This shows how fearful the sight of this army was to the lands toward which it was moving, and also God's overwhelming power over this great army, in addition to the abundance of the spoil from which the children of God benefit when they triumph over this army. It is to be noted that the camels and other beasts, such as donkeys and mules, were for carrying personal baggage such as tents, clothing and the tools of daily living, in addition to spare weapons.

2.6.1.en: Because Syria was distinguished by its cultivation of wheat, he commanded that the grain be gathered from its farms when he attacked it and took possession of its cities, so that it would meet the needs of the army, which needs at least forty tons of wheat daily for its food.

2.6.2.en: From this we understand how confident Holofernes was that he would triumph over all the lands he would meet and take possession of their spoil and their crops. He was very conceited and relied on the strength of his army.

2.7.0.en: King Nabuchodonosor gave Holofernes countless quantities of gold and silver to pay the salaries of the officers and soldiers, so that their morale would be high and they would fight bravely in their wars.

2.7.1.en: If man knows how to gather the needs of his journeys on earth from various material things, do you prepare what your journey to heaven requires, of spiritual worship, prayers, fasts and all works of mercy? And do you prepare the spiritual weapon, to overcome the wars of the devil and subdue him under your feet, so that you reach your goal, which is the Kingdom? I wish that you would not be sparing toward yourself in any spiritual striving, to ensure your victory, and God will help you according to your concern and your love for Him.

2.8.s.en: (3) The devastation of the surrounding lands

2.8.1.en: After preparing the great army, Holofernes began to move out of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, where King Nebuchadnezzar dwelt. The army included foot soldiers and horsemen, with bows and arrows, and the riders of the war chariots. Their number was very great, covering several kilometers, so they resembled swarms of locusts that cover vast areas when they attack any country.

2.9.0.en: Assyria: a kingdom located in the north of Iraq, which expanded and extended to include almost the whole world of that time. Here the kingdom of Assyria before its expansion is meant.

2.9.1.en: The great mountains of Ange: a mountain range located in the west of Asia Minor, that is, western Turkey.

2.9.2.en: He describes here in general what this great army reached. It moved out of Nineveh and swept through many lands until it reached Turkey and the great mountains of Ange, on which many fortresses had been built, and it was able to take possession of all these lands; even these fortresses fell into its hand.

2.9.3.en: Put: a large city located in western Turkey.

2.9.4.en: The children of Tharsis: tribes that dwelt mostly in the wilderness of western Turkey, then migrated and settled in southern Spain.

2.9.5.en: The children of Ishmael: tribes that dwelt in the Arabian Peninsula, then migrated to dwell in the wilderness of western Turkey, and they had many herds.

2.9.6.en: Chelon: a city located in southern Turkey.

2.9.7.en: He lists here the lands that Holofernes took possession of. He destroyed and occupied many cities and places in western Turkey, such as Put, the children of Tharsis, the children of Ishmael and the land of Chelon.

2.10.0.en: Euphrates: a great river in Iraq.

2.10.2.en: The valley of Mambre: in southern Palestine, east of the Mediterranean Sea; it was also called the city of Hebron, in which Abraham dwelt.

2.10.3.en: He mentions here other lands that Holofernes took possession of, which lie between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates in Iraq. He also took possession of lands in southern Palestine, such as the valley of Mambre. We note that the writer here is not bound to the route of the army, but mentions the various lands the army took possession of, until the whole world was subject to Nabuchodonosor. He mentions here some of the lands and not all of them, and he singles out the strong fortified lands, or the peoples and regions from which he took his needs, such as the cattle from the children of Tharsis and the children of Ishmael, and the wheat and barley from Syria. This explains the difference between the list of lands mentioned in this chapter and the one mentioned in the previous chapter, for he does not mention here all the lands he took possession of, but only some of them.

2.11.0.en: The borders of Japheth which are toward the south: they lie south of the Caspian Sea and the Black Sea as far as western Turkey.

2.11.1.en: He took possession of many lands lying on the southern borders of Japheth, which are northeast of Nineveh as far as the north of the Mediterranean Sea in the west.

2.12.0.en: The children of Madian: the inhabitants of Midian, which lies east of the Gulf of Aqaba.

2.12.1.en: He also took possession of the tribes of Midian and took their spoil of many herds, and killed everyone of them who opposed him.

2.13.0.en: He went to the lands of Syria and took from them the wheat, the crops and the fruits, and that was in the days of harvest, that is, about the month of May. This means that he continued this campaign for more than a year, for he began his campaign when he went out from Nineveh in the month of April (ch. 1), and it is unreasonable that he took possession of all these lands within two months, so this expedition took more than a year. And after he had taken his needs of grain, he burned the rest of the fields and the trees, to weaken these lands so that they would become subject to him.

2.14.0.en: So we see that this army was very fearful in all the lands of the world, so they submitted to it, and the resistance was very weak, not worth mentioning.

2.14.1.en: So the devil displays his material power to terrify the hearts of the children of God, but he is powerless before those who believe in the power of God, so he fears them and trembles if they are confident in their God. And the devil, if he could, would destroy our whole life cruelly, for our enemy, as the Holy Bible says, is "as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour" (1 Pet 5:8), but he cannot, because "If God be for us, who can be against us?" (Rom 8:31). The complete submission to Holofernes
